ARTICLE: Spin bowling
WIKIPEDIA REVISION TEXT
======================================================================

{{Short description|Bowling technique in cricket}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2016}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2026}}
{{Bowling techniques sidebar |expanded=all}}
[[File:Muralitharan bowling to Adam Gilchrist.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Spin bowler [[Muttiah Muralitharan]] bowling to the batsman, [[Adam Gilchrist]]]]
'''Spin bowling''' is a [[bowling (cricket)|bowling]] technique in [[cricket]], in which the ball is [[Delivery (cricket)|delivered]] relatively slowly but with rapid [[rotation]], giving it the potential to deviate sharply after bouncing. A bowler who uses this technique is called a '''spinner''',<ref name="Marks">{{cite web |last=Marks |first=Vic |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2022/mar/04/the-greatest-spinner-ive-ever-seen-and-an-incredibly-generous-cricketer |title=Warne was the greatest spinner I've seen and an incredibly generous cricketer |work=The Guardian |date=4 March 2022 |access-date=8 November 2024 |quote=He started under Marsh's wing at the Adelaide academy before graduating in spectacular fashion to become the greatest spin bowler I've ever seen}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Thomas |first=Richard |date=30 March 2020 |title=The Ten: Mystery Spinners |url=https://www.wisden.com/cricket-features/the-ten-mystery-spinners-all-out-cricket |access-date=9 April 2025 |work=Wisden |quote=The art of spin-bowling in cricket probably demands more precision than any other area of expertise in the game. Despite bowling attacks being primarily loaded by quicks, the spinners, since the game's inception have been the much sought after weapons for fielding captains.}}</ref> a '''spin bowler''',<ref name="Marks"/> or a '''slow bowler'''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Brearley |first=Mike |date=23 October 2023 |title=Bishan Singh Bedi: 'The most beautiful of slow bowlers' – Mike Brearley, Almanack |url=https://www.wisden.com/wisden-cricketers-almanack/bishan-singh-bedi-the-most-beautiful-of-slow-bowlers-mike-brearley-almanack |access-date=9 April 2025 |work=Wisden |quote=The first epithet that comes to mind for Bishan Singh Bedi's bowling is "beautiful". More than with any other slow bowler, this is the word that stays.}}</ref>

It is one of the two main approaches to bowling, the other being [[fast bowling]].

A spinner may bowl with their right-arm or left-arm, and with a [[finger spin]] or [[wrist spin]] action. Therefore, there are four types of spin bowling: [[off spin]], [[leg spin]], [[left-arm orthodox spin]] and [[left-arm unorthodox spin]].

The bowlers with the highest, second-highest and fourth-highest number of [[Dismissal (cricket)|wickets]] in the history of [[Test cricket]], [[Muttiah Muralitharan]], [[Shane Warne]] and [[Anil Kumble]], respectively, were spinners.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://stats.espncricinfo.com/ci/content/records/93276.html|title=Records / Test matches / Bowling records / Most wickets in career|publisher=ESPNcricinfo|access-date=7 November 2024}}</ref>

==Purpose==
The main aim of spin bowling is to bowl the [[cricket ball]] with rapid rotation so that when it [[bouncing ball|bounces]] on the [[cricket pitch|pitch]] it will deviate from its normal straight path, thus making it difficult for the [[batsman]] to hit the ball cleanly.<ref name="Dummies">Knight, pp.122–123.</ref> The speed the ball travels is not critical, and is significantly slower than that for [[fast bowling]]. A typical spin delivery has a speed in the range 70–90&nbsp;km/h (45–55&nbsp;mph).

==Techniques==
[[Image:Off break small.gif|frame|right|An off-spin delivery by (right arm over the wicket)]]
[[Image:Leg break small.gif|frame|right|A leg-spin delivery by (right arm over the wicket)]]

Spin bowling is divided into four categories, depending on the physical technique used. There is virtually no overlap between the two basic biomechanical techniques of [[wrist spin]] and [[finger spin]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://cricketsecrets.com/2010/08/spin-bowling-tip/| title= Spin Bowling Tips| date= 11 December 2010|publisher=CricketSecrets.com|access-date=4 February 2015}}</ref>

Depending on technique, a spin bowler uses either predominant wrist or finger motion to impart spin to the ball around a horizontal axis that is at an oblique angle to the length of the pitch. This sort of spin means it is also possible for the [[Magnus effect]] to cause the ball to deviate sideways through the air, before it bounces. Such deviation is called ''drift''.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://spinbowlingtips.com/drift/|title= Drift| publisher=SpinBowlingTips.com|access-date=4 February 2015}}</ref> The combination of drift and spin can make the ball's trajectory complex, with a change of direction at the bounce.

Spin bowlers are generally given the task of bowling with an old, worn cricket ball. A new cricket ball better suits the techniques of fast bowling than spin bowling, while a worn one grips the pitch better and achieves greater spin.<ref name="Dummies" /> Spin bowlers are also more effective later in a game, as the pitch dries up and begins to crack and crumble. This again provides more purchase for the spinning ball and produces greater deviation. Spin bowlers that open the bowling are rare, but became a more viable option with the introduction of [[Twenty20 cricket]] when pitch conditions are in their favour, and the ball also generally drifts more in the air. Spin bowlers can also be used tactically in shorter forms of the game, to 'take the pace off the ball'. This strategy is especially effective to slow down the scoring rates of batsmen who specialise in making use of the pace of faster bowlers to score runs quickly. The lower inherent momentum of a spin bowler necessitates more power exerted by the batsman to achieve the same results.

==Equivalences==
Both finger spin and wrist spin bowlers use a range of different angles of spin to confuse the batsman and dismiss them. Many of these variations have direct equivalents in the other discipline, but the names used for the various deliveries may be different.

==Conditions==
Spin bowling has become a forte of bowlers from South Asia. The primary reason for this is that pitches in the sub-continent provide more help to spin bowlers. The faster the pitch degenerates, the earlier the spinners come into the picture. Australian and South African pitches are usually very hard and bouncy, helping the fast bowlers more. They do not break up very much during the match. In contrast, pitches in the sub-continent are not that hard. They are not usually held together by the grass as much; hence they break up more quickly and help spin bowlers.

In addition to this, spin bowling is considered to be less tiring than pace bowling as it generally does not employ a lengthy run up. Therefore, spin bowling is more prevalent in the hot and humid conditions of the sub-continent as a form of energy conservation, especially in multi-day competitions.

In general, leg-spin is considered to be one of the toughest types of bowling in which to keep control of the ball, but it is very effective in picking off wickets.<ref>Bob Woolmer "The Art and Science of Cricket"</ref>

==Flight, turn, bounce, drift, dip==
[[File:Cricket-Spin-Bounce.jpg|thumb|Bounce]]
[[File:Cricket-Spin-Drift.jpg|thumb|upright=0.5|Drift]]
[[File:Cricket-Spin-Dip.jpg|thumb|Dip]]
[[File:Cricket-Spin-Flight.jpg|thumb|Flight]]

It is customary among cricket commentators to describe and judge the quality of spin bowling in terms of the characteristics ''flight'', ''turn'', ''bounce'', ''drift'', and ''dip''. All these are arts to deceive the batsman and require much practice. The basic trajectory of spin bowling is two-lines-at-an-angle, but the above characteristics (described below) modify this 'normal' trajectory into more complex shapes.

'''Turn''': How much the ball turns after pitching (e.g. 5 degree deviation after meeting the ground). It depends on the number and direction of revolutions of the ball.  The movement and rotation of the ball varies, depending on the position of the wrist and the finger. An occasional unexpected straight ball can usefully be included in an attack, but spin variation is the main technique used to deceive the batsman and take wickets. A high rate of turn is above 33 rev/second, or 2000 rpm. [[Graeme Swann]] consistently spun over 2000 rpm, the most amongst English spinners until [[Liam Dawson]] topped 35 rev/second, or 2100 rpm. Also, the slower the ball, the more it tends to deviate. For an offspinner, you will have to bowl from wide of off-stump to get the ball to turn into the right-handed batsman and force them to nick off the edge to a fielder or into the top of off stump.

'''Bounce''': Getting the ball to bounce more than normal, so that the ball meets the batsman at a greater height than expected. Sometimes, if the ball spins horizontally (e.g. a slider), the batsman will not be able to make contact with the ball and it may hit the stumps before the second bounce.

'''Drift''': Getting the ball to move sideways while in air. Late drift causes the batsman to cover the wrong line and the ball may catch the edge of the bat.

'''Dip''': Getting the ball to pitch (meet the ground) at a shorter distance than normal. Late dip causes the batsman to misjudge the length of the ball.

[[Flight (cricket)|'''Flight''']]: throwing the ball up a bit more than normal, so that its time in the air before pitching is longer. A slow ball with extra flight may deceive the batsman into thinking it is slower than it is and therefore mistiming his shot. This is very effective for offspinners. Usually a spin bowler relies on tricks during flight to produce turn, bounce, drift and dip, or combinations of them.

'''Test cricket''' is a [[Forms of cricket|format]] of the sport of [[cricket]], considered the game's most prestigious and traditional form. Often referred to as the "ultimate test" of a cricketer's skill, endurance and temperament, it is a [[First-class cricket|first-class]] format of international cricket where two teams in [[Cricket whites|whites]], each representing their country, compete over a match that can last up to five days. It consists of up to four [[innings]] (up to two per team), with a minimum of ninety [[Over (cricket)|overs]] scheduled to be bowled in six hours per day, making it the sport with the longest playing time except for some multi-stage cycling races. A team wins the match by outscoring the opposition with the [[Batting (cricket)|bat]] and bowling them out with the [[Bowling (cricket)|ball]]. Otherwise the match ends in a [[Result (cricket)|draw]].

It is contested by 12 teams which are the [[List of International Cricket Council members|full-members]] of the [[International Cricket Council]] (ICC). The term "test match" was originally coined in 1861–62 but in a different context—that the English team was testing itself against all of the Australian colonies.<ref name="Cricket1970">{{cite book |last=Bowen |first=Rowland |author-link=Rowland Bowen |title=Cricket: A History of its Growth and Development |publisher=Eyre & Spottiswoode |year=1970 |isbn=978-04-13278-60-9 |location=London |page=99}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Dying? Like hell it is - Long live Test cricket |url=https://archive.sen.com.au/news/2023/02/28/dying-like-hell-it-is-long-live-test-cricket |access-date=2 August 2025 |website=archive.sen.com.au |language=en }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Test cricket did not become an officially recognised format until the 1890s, but many international matches since 1877 have been retrospectively awarded Test status. The first such match took place at the [[Melbourne Cricket Ground]] (MCG) in March 1877 between teams which were then known as a Combined Australian XI and [[James Lillywhite]]'s XI, the latter a team of visiting English professionals. Matches between [[Australia national cricket team|Australia]] and [[England cricket team|England]] were first called "test matches" in 1892. The first definitive list of retrospective Tests was written by South Australian journalist [[Clarence P. Moody]] two years later and, by the end of the century, had gained acceptance.

Traditionally, Test matches had always been played with a red ball during daylight hours. However, amid growing concern over dwindling viewership in the late 2000s, numerous trials were held in the early 2010s which culminated in [[Day/night cricket|day/night Tests]] being permitted by the ICC in 2012, and the first day/night match was between [[New Zealand cricket team in Australia in 2015–16|Australia and New Zealand]] at the [[Adelaide Oval]] in November 2015. These matches start later in the day and continue into the evening, necessitating the use of a pink ball to aid visibility.

The [[World Test Championship|ICC World Test Championship]] is the [[World cup competition|international championship]] of Test cricket. It is a league competition run by the ICC, with its inaugural season starting in [[2019–2021 World Test Championship|2019]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Schedule for inaugural World Test Championship announced |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/news/742337 |publisher=International Cricket Council |access-date=2 March 2024 |archive-date=4 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181204204916/https://www.icc-cricket.com/news/742337 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=Ramsey, Andrew |date=20 June 2018 |title=Aussies to host Afghans as part of new schedule |url=https://www.cricket.com.au/news/icc-future-tour-program-schedule-fixture-international-cricket-ftp-australia-afghanistan-india/2018-06-20 |website=[[cricket.com.au]] |access-date=2 March 2024 |archive-date=20 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180620180802/https://www.cricket.com.au/news/icc-future-tour-program-schedule-fixture-international-cricket-ftp-australia-afghanistan-india/2018-06-20 |url-status=live }}</ref> In line with the ICC's goal of having one pinnacle tournament for each of the three formats of international cricket, it is the premier championship for Test cricket.<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 June 2013 |title=Test Championship to replace Champions Trophy |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci-icc/content/story/646147.html |publisher=ESPNcricinfo |access-date=2 March 2024 |archive-date=20 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180620182116/http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci-icc/content/story/646147.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Early history==
{{main|History of cricket|History of Test cricket from 1877 to 1883|History of Test cricket from 1884 to 1889|History of Test cricket from 1890 to 1900}}

===Growth of international cricket===
Teams designated as "England" or "All England" began to play in the 18th century, but these teams were not truly representative. Early [[international cricket]] was disrupted by the [[French Revolution]] and the [[American Civil War]]. The earliest international cricket match was between [[Canadian cricket team in the United States in 1844|the United States and Canada]], on 24 and 26 September 1844 (bad weather prevented play on the 25th).<ref>[http://www.espncricinfo.com/usa/engine/match/318995.html United States of America v Canada 1844] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629061551/http://www.espncricinfo.com/usa/engine/match/318995.html |date=29 June 2011 }}. ESPNcricinfo.</ref> Overseas tours by national English teams began in 1859 with visits to North America, Australia and New Zealand. The [[Australian Aboriginal cricket team in England in 1868|1868 Australian Aboriginals]] were the first organised overseas team to tour England.

[[File:Ashes Urn 1921.jpg|left|thumb|The earliest published photo of [[the Ashes urn]], from ''[[The Illustrated London News]]'', 1921]]
Two rival English tours of Australia were proposed in the early months of 1877, with [[James Lillywhite]] campaigning for a professional tour and [[Fred Grace]] for an amateur one. Grace's tour fell through and it was Lillywhite's team that toured New Zealand and Australia in 1876–77. Two matches against a combined Australian XI were later classified as the first official Test matches. The first match was won by Australia, by 45 runs and the second by England. After reciprocal tours established a pattern of international cricket, [[The Ashes]] was established as a competition during the Australian tour of England in 1882. A surprise victory for Australia inspired a mock obituary of English cricket to be published in the ''Sporting Times'' the following day: the phrase "The body shall be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia" prompted the subsequent creation of the Ashes urn.

The series of 1884–85 was the first to be held over five matches: England player [[Alfred Shaw]], writing in 1901, considered the side to be "the best ever to have left England". South Africa became the third team to play Test cricket in 1888–89, when they hosted a tour by an under-strength England side. Australia, England and South Africa were the only countries playing Test cricket before [[World War I]].

===Terminology===
The term "test match" was coined during the [[English cricket team in Australia in 1861–62|English tour of Australia in 1861–62]] but in a different context. It meant that the English team was testing itself against each of the Australian colonies.<ref name="Cricket1970" /> Following Lillywhite's tour, Australian teams reciprocated, beginning with [[Australian cricket team in England and North America in 1878|Dave Gregory's team in 1878]]. By the beginning of 1892, eight English teams had visited Australia and seven Australian teams had visited England. In its issue of 25 February 1892, ''[[Cricket: A Weekly Record of the Game]]'' revived the term "test match" and freely applied it to the [[English cricket team in Australia in 1891–92|three international matches]] which had just been played in Australia by [[Henry Holroyd, 3rd Earl of Sheffield|Lord Sheffield's XI]], starting with the match at the MCG which was billed as Lord Sheffield's Team v Combined Australia. The report began: "There was no little appropriateness in fixing the first of the three great test matches for January 1".<ref name="C29127">[https://archive.acscricket.com/cricket/1892/33/ "Tenth Match – Lord Sheffield's Team v Combined Australia"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908221801/https://archive.acscricket.com/cricket/1892/33/ |date=8 September 2022 }} ''Cricket'', issue 291, 25 February 1892, p. 27.</ref>

===Clarence P. Moody===
The first list of matches considered to be "Tests" was conceived and published by South Australian journalist [[Clarence P. Moody]] in his 1894 book, ''Australian Cricket and Cricketers, 1856 to 1893–94''. Moody's proposal was well received by [[Charles W. Alcock]], editor of ''Cricket'' in England and his list of 39 matches was reproduced in the 28 December 1894 issue as part of an article entitled "The First Test Match". The list begins with the [[Melbourne Cricket Ground|MCG]] match played 15–17 March 1877 and ends with the recent match at the [[Sydney Cricket Ground|Association Ground, Sydney]] played 14–20 December 1894.<ref name="C379463">[https://archive.acscricket.com/cricket/1894/487/ "The First Test Match"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908225143/https://archive.acscricket.com/cricket/1894/487/ |date=8 September 2022 }} ''Cricket'', issue 379, 28 December 1894, pp. 463–464.</ref> All 39 were retrospectively recognised as Test matches, as was the unlisted 1890 [[Old Trafford Cricket Ground|Old Trafford]] match that was abandoned without a ball being bowled. No South African matches were included in Moody's list but three against England were also given retrospective Test status.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Records/England/Test/Team/List_of_Matches.html |title=List of Test Matches |work=CricketArchive |access-date=9 September 2022 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=9 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220909044131/https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Records/England/Test/Team/List_of_Matches.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Moody became a newspaper editor and founded the Adelaide ''[[Sunday Mail (Adelaide)|Sunday Mail]]'' in 1912.<ref>[https://www.adelaidenow.com.au/news/game-on-a-rich-sporting-history/news-story/07eca80e5030e130571aad9044d9362d "Game on: a rich sporting history"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220908230423/https://www.adelaidenow.com.au/news/game-on-a-rich-sporting-history/news-story/07eca80e5030e130571aad9044d9362d |date=8 September 2022 }}. Hilferty, Tim: ''The Advertiser''. 5 May 2012.</ref>

== Twentieth century ==

=== Further growth and creation of the Imperial Cricket Conference (ICC) ===
Growth of Tests continued, with 48 being played from 1901 to 1910.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Test Cricket – List of Matches for 1901 to 1910 |url=https://howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Matches/MatchList.asp?Group=1900010119101231&Range=1900%20to%201910 |access-date=10 August 2025 |website=www.howstat.com}}</ref> The [[Imperial Cricket Conference]] (ICC) was founded on 15 July 1909, with England, Australia and South Africa as the founding members. The ICC included the [[Marylebone Cricket Club]] (MCC), the [[Cricket Australia|Australian Board of Control for International Cricket]], and the [[Cricket South Africa|South African Cricket Association]] as its original associations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Gupta |first=Amit |title=The Oxford handbook of sports history |date=2017 |others={{ill|Robert Edelman|de}}, Wayne Wilson |isbn=978-0-19-985891-0 |location=New York, NY |pages=214–215 |chapter=14-Cricket: The Indianization of an Imperial Game |oclc=959032235}}</ref> The ICC would oversee and regulate cricket between these three countries.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Iyer |first=Usha |date=September 2013 |title=Decolonisation and the Imperial Cricket Conference, 1947–1965: A Study in Transnational Commonwealth History? |url=https://clok.uclan.ac.uk/id/eprint/9659/1/Iyer%20Usha%20Final%20e-Thesis%20%28Master%20Copy%29.pdf |access-date=9 August 2025}}</ref> The President and Secretary of the MCC subsequently became the President and Secretary of the ICC. [[Lord's]], the home of the MCC, hence became the headquarters of the ICC. At their 1909 meeting, the ICC instigated a [[1912 Triangular Tournament|triangular tournament to be held between the three countries in 1912]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The original damp squib |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-the-1912-triangular-tournament-in-england-465748 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240225231623/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-the-1912-triangular-tournament-in-england-465748 |archive-date=25 February 2024 |access-date=9 August 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> The nine-match tournament was marred by rain, and combined with the three-day match length for Tests in England at the time meant six of the matches resulted in draws. The tournament was so unsuccessful that the idea was never attempted again. The Daily Telegraph noted: "Nine Tests provide a surfeit of cricket, and contests between Australia and South Africa are not a great attraction to the British public."

There were only 24 Tests between 1911 and 1920,<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Test Cricket – List of Matches for 1910 to 1920 |url=https://howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Matches/MatchList.asp?Group=1911010119201231&v=D&Range=1911%20to%201920 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250320055853/https://howstat.com/Cricket/Statistics/Matches/MatchList.asp?Group=1911010119201231&v=M&Range=1911%20to%201920 |archive-date=20 March 2025 |access-date=9 August 2025 |website=www.howstat.com |language=en}}</ref> including the nine as part of the 1912 Triangular Tournament, owing to the disruption caused by [[World War I]]. When Test cricket resumed after the war, England was the first to tour Australia as part of the [[English cricket team in Australia in 1920–21|1920–21 Ashes Series]], who were [[Whitewash (sport)|whitewashed]] by Australia for the first time in a Test series.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Ebor |first=Old |date=14 January 2019 |title="They have whacked us, well": JWHT Douglas and the Ashes whitewash |url=https://oldebor.wordpress.com/2019/01/14/they-have-whacked-us-well/ |access-date=9 August 2025 |website=Old Ebor |language=en |archive-date=13 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250913211507/https://oldebor.wordpress.com/2019/01/14/they-have-whacked-us-well/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":3">Burton S (2021) [https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2021/mar/02/the-1920-21-ashes-typhus-quarantine-and-unseemly-barracking The 1920–21 Ashes: typhus quarantine and unseemly barracking], ''[[The Guardian]]'', 2 March 2021. Retrieved 2 March 2021.</ref> England were required to quarantine before the series due to an outbreak of typhus on their ship, and also had injuries to key players, which disrupted their preparation.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> After the conclusion of the series, England's captain [[Johnny Douglas]] congratulated the Australians "who have whacked us, well."<ref name=":2" />

The ICC held a second meeting in 1921 which focused on the use of eight-ball overs.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=icc |title=1909–1963 – Imperial Cricket Conference {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1909-1963 |access-date=9 August 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=22 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240222135726/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1909-1963 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Admission of India, New Zealand and West Indies ===
India, New Zealand and West Indies were invited to attend the ICC's third meeting on 31 May 1926, and subsequently became full members on the same day.<ref name=":4" /> At the meeting, it was agreed that the membership of the ICC should comprise "governing bodies of cricket in countries within the Empire to which cricket teams are sent, or which send teams to England." This definition regrettably excluded the United States, which had regularly received teams from England since 1859 and had also sent several teams to play in England.<ref name=":5" /> The meeting also discussed the "farcical" limit of three days for Tests, and it was unanimously agreed to establish an allotment of "more than three days for tests [sic] in England, which should be played out if possible." The MCC representatives confirmed that the English counties would be consulted in regard to the Australian proposal that at least four days should be permitted for Test matches.<ref>{{Cite news |date=9 June 1926 |title=CRICKET CONFERENCE |url=https://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article16297499 |access-date=10 August 2025 |work=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] |location=New South Wales, Australia |page=15 |via=National Library of Australia |issue=27,590}}</ref> The meeting further discussed the use of eight-ball overs, and heard that all the State Cricket Associations in Australia had been consulted by the Australian Board of Control, with a unanimous decision that the eight-ball over was in the best interests of the game.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1 June 1926 |title=CRICKET CONFERENCE |url=https://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article163384090 |access-date=10 August 2025 |work=[[The Newcastle Sun]] |location=New South Wales, Australia |page=5 |via=National Library of Australia |issue=2649}}</ref>

From this point onward, the ICC met "on an almost annual basis" except during war years, to set out future Test tours, checking that players were properly qualified, and encouraging the use of turf instead of matting pitches. Possible law changes were also discussed.<ref name=":5" />

West Indies toured England for their Test debut on 23 June 1928 against England at Lord's as part of a [[West Indian cricket team in England in 1928|three-Test series]]. England won each match batting only once, with the West Indies being largely outplayed. However they had shown their huge potential in a series of reciprocal tours in the previous decade.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Williamson |first=Martin |date=1 February 2014 |title=Playing two Tests in a day |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-to-1930-when-england-played-two-tests-in-a-day-714423 |access-date=11 August 2025 |website=ESPNCricinfo |archive-date=18 August 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250818043214/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-to-1930-when-england-played-two-tests-in-a-day-714423 |url-status=live }}</ref>

New Zealand made their Test debut on 10 January 1930 at [[Lancaster Park]] as England toured New Zealand for a [[English cricket team in New Zealand in 1929–30|three-Test series]]. Due a quirk of scheduling the series between previously agreed tours (Australia in 1928[[English cricket team in Australia in 1920–21|–]]29 & 1932–33 and South Africa in 1930–31), England was also playing a four-Test series against the [[English cricket team in the West Indies in 1929–30|West Indies at the same time]].<ref name=":6" /> Due to the third Test of the England-New Zealand series being affected by rain, a fourth was arranged to start on 21 February 1930 at [[Eden Park]]. The third Test of the England-West Indies series also began on the same day at [[Bourda]]. It was the only time one country has played in two Test matches on the same day.<ref>{{cite web |title=Quick, quick Snow |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/magazine/content/story/149452.html |access-date=14 January 2020 |work=ESPN Cricinfo |archive-date=3 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203061506/http://www.espncricinfo.com/magazine/content/story/149452.html |url-status=live }}</ref> England won the New Zealand series 1–0, with three draws.

The fourth Test of the England-West Indies series was [[Timeless Test|timeless]]. England made 849 from 259 overs in the first innings, with [[Andy Sandham]] scoring 325, then the world record score; it was also the first Test triple century.<ref name=":6" /> England bowled the West Indies out for 286 from 111.5 overs, establishing a first-innings lead of 563. England's captain, [[Freddie Calthorpe|Calthorpe]], was criticised for not enforcing the follow-on, but the age of his side was likely a major factor.<ref name=":6" /> England thus batted again, notching 272 from 79.1 overs before declaring 9 wickets down.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scorecard – 1929–1930 West Indies v England – 03/04/1930 |url=http://www.howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Matches/MatchScorecard.asp?MatchCode=0193 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230422071433/http://www.howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Matches/MatchScorecard.asp?MatchCode=0193 |archive-date=22 April 2023 |access-date=11 August 2025 |website=howstat.com |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> With time seemingly unlimited, the West Indies were set 836 to win. At the close of play on the seventh day, they had scored 408 runs for the loss of five wickets, but two days of rain followed. As was the case with the infamous [[English cricket team in South Africa in 1938–39|Durban match in 1939]], England's ship was departing and the game had to finish a draw.<ref name=":6" />

India [[Indian cricket team in England in 1932|toured England for their debut in Tests]] on 25 June 1932. England won the only Test by 158 runs.

=== Changes to the size of the wicket ===
[[File:Reggie Schwarz c1905.jpg|thumb|278x278px|Reggie Schwarz in c. 1905 showing the smaller wicket]]In 1931, provisions were added to Law 6 in the [[Laws of Cricket]] to alter the size of the wicket (stumps and bails).<ref>{{Cite web |title=A brief history of cricket |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/a-brief-history-of-cricket-239757 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250708080316/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/a-brief-history-of-cricket-239757 |archive-date=8 July 2025 |access-date=10 August 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> The text was changed from the 1927 version which was as follows:<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |title=The ACS – The ACS |url=https://acscricket.com/ |access-date=10 August 2025 |language=en-GB |archive-date=23 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250923220633/https://acscricket.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=Each wicket shall be eight inches in width and consist of three stumps, with two bails upon the top. The stumps shall be of equal and sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, twenty-seven inches out of the ground.}}

In the 1931 revision, the relevant text was as follows:<ref name="auto"/>

{{Blockquote|text=Each wicket shall be not less than eight inches and no more than nine inches in width and consist of three stumps, with two bails upon the top. The stumps shall be of equal and sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, not less than twenty-seven inches nor more than twenty-eight inches out of the ground.}}

Later, Law 6, which became Law 8, was standardised in the 1947 revision to the larger size as follows:<ref>{{Cite web |title=The ACS – The ACS |url=https://acscricket.com/ |access-date=10 August 2025 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

{{Blockquote|text=Each Wicket shall be 9 inches in width and consist of three stumps with two bails upon the top. The stumps shall be of equal and of sufficient size to prevent the ball from passing through, with their top 28 inches above the ground.|source=}}

=== The genesis and outlawing of bodyline ===
{{Main|Bodyline}}

==== 1930 Ashes series ====

After [[Don Bradman|Bradman]] scored 974 runs at an average of 139.14 (with four centuries – 131, 254, 334 and 232) in the [[Australian cricket team in England in 1930|1930 Ashes series]] in England, the most runs ever scored in a series—a record that still stands to this day,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Test matches {{!}} Batting records {{!}} Most runs in a series {{!}} ESPNcricinfo |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/records/most-runs-in-a-series-282849 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250120191729/https://www.espncricinfo.com/records/most-runs-in-a-series-282849 |archive-date=20 January 2025 |access-date=11 August 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> the English sought to curtail his impact. In the timeless 5th Test where he made 232, a number of English players and commentators had noted Bradman's discomfort in playing the [[Bouncer (cricket)|short, rising delivery]].<ref name="Sportsfactor">{{cite web |date=2 March 2001 |title=The Sports Factor (transcript) |url=http://www.abc.net.au/rn/sportsfactor/stories/2001/253062.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080205083438/http://www.abc.net.au/rn/sportsfactor/stories/2001/253062.htm |archive-date=5 February 2008 |access-date=23 August 2008 |work=ABC Radio}}</ref> The observation was made too late to have an impact on the match, which Australia won by an innings and 39 runs, which also meant Australia won the series 2–1.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ENG vs AUS Cricket Scorecard, 5th Test at London, August 16–22, 1930 |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/series/australia-tour-of-england-1930-61334/england-vs-australia-5th-test-62584/full-scorecard |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250615051325/https://www.espncricinfo.com/series/australia-tour-of-england-1930-61334/england-vs-australia-5th-test-62584/full-scorecard |archive-date=15 June 2025 |access-date=11 August 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> Wisden made of a period of play:<ref>{{cite web |year=1931 |title=Fifth Test Match: England v Australia 1930 |url=http://content-aus.cricinfo.com/wisdenalmanack/content/story/151746.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120708060750/http://content-aus.cricinfo.com/wisdenalmanack/content/story/151746.html |archive-date=8 July 2012 |access-date=23 May 2008 |work=Wisden}}</ref>{{blockquote|On the Wednesday morning the ball flew about a good deal, both batsmen frequently being hit on the body&nbsp;... on more than one occasion each player cocked the ball up dangerously but always, as it happened, just wide of the fieldsmen.}}The revelation provided England with a possible tactic for the next Ashes series in [[English cricket team in Australia in 1932–33|Australia in 1932–33]]. England's new captain, [[Douglas Jardine]], along with his bowlers, devised and practised a plan in the [[1932 English cricket season|1932 season]] called "fast leg theory" which later became known as [[bodyline]]. It involved bowling at leg stump or just outside, and pitching the ball short, so that once bounced it reared up threateningly at the body of a batsman standing in an orthodox batting position. Fielders positioned on the leg side would catch any defensive deflection off the bat.<ref name="D103">Douglas, p. 103.</ref><ref name="BBC">{{cite web |last1=Watson |first1=Greig |date=16 January 2013 |title=Bodyline: 80 years of cricket's greatest controversy |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-21013615 |access-date=21 October 2017 |publisher=BBC |archive-date=19 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171019231812/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-nottinghamshire-21013615 |url-status=live }}</ref> The batsman's options were limited as [[Batting (cricket)#Pull and hook|pull or hook shots]] could be caught on the boundary and defensive shots brought few runs and could carry far enough to the keeper or leg-side fielders. Other options included evading the ball through ducking or moving aside, or allowing the ball to strike the body.<ref name="pi130">Piesse, p. 130.</ref><ref name="h70">Haigh and Frith, p. 70.</ref><ref name="c171">Colman, p. 171.</ref>

==== 1932–33 Ashes series ====
[[File:Bodyline_Cricket_Series_1932_SLNSW_FL1660012.jpg|thumb|Jardine leads the English Team onto the Sydney Cricket Ground, 2 December 1932]]England employed bodyline in the 1932–33 series, with the tactic causing huge controversy due to its unsportsmanlike nature and restriction of scoring options. In the third Test at Adelaide, a spell of bowling from [[Harold Larwood]] saw [[Bill Woodfull]] struck over the heart. He dropped his bat, and staggered away holding his chest, bent over in pain. Jardine called to Larwood: "Well bowled, Harold!". Although the comment was aimed at unsettling Bradman, who was also batting at the time, Woodfull was appalled.<ref>Hamilton, p. 156.</ref><ref>Frith, p. 179.</ref> Play later resumed when Woodfull was fit to continue, and Allen bowled the next over. Play was again stopped for Larwood's next over when the players were moved into bodyline positions, as the crowd protested and called abuse at the England team. Many commentators condemned the field change as unsporting, and the furious spectators became extremely volatile.<ref name="F181">Frith, p. 181.</ref>

Following the fourth day's play at Adelaide, the Australian Board of Control sent a telegraph to the MCC, cricket's ruling body and the club that selected the England team. The Australian Board had claimed bodyline was unsportsmanlike and that the bowling was menacing the best interests of the game. Meanwhile, the match continued and saw England bowled out for 412 on day five, setting Australia a target of 532 to win. Australia only had significant contributions from Woodfull, 73 from 208 balls, Bradman, 66 from 71 balls, and [[Vic Richardson]], 21 from 76 balls, as they were bowled out for 193 inside 70 overs on the sixth day. England were 2–1 up in the series.

The MCC replied to the first telegraph the following week, deeply resenting the accusation of unsportsmanlike bowling. Additionally, members of the MCC believed that the Australians had over-reacted to the English bowling.<ref name="BBC"/> At this point, the remainder of the series was under threat.<ref name="p259">Pollard, p. 259.</ref><ref>Frith, p. 227.</ref> [[File:4th Test Woodfull.jpg|thumb|[[Bill Woodfull]] evades a bodyline ball]]The Australian Board then sent another cable on 30 January, indicating that they wished the series to continue and offering to postpone consideration of the fairness of bodyline bowling until after the series. The MCC replied on 2 February, suggesting that continuing the series would be impossible unless the accusation of unsporting behaviour was withdrawn.<ref>Frith, pp. 226–28.</ref> The affair rose to the political level, and it was believed that it could have a significant trade impact between the two nations. The standoff was settled when [[Prime Minister of Australia|the Australian prime minister]], [[Joseph Lyons]], met with members of the Australian Board and outlined to them the severe economic hardships that could be caused in Australia if the British public boycotted Australian trade. Following considerable discussion and debate in the English and Australian press, the Australian Board sent a cable to the MCC which, while maintaining its opposition to bodyline bowling, stated "We do not regard the sportsmanship of your team as being in question".<ref name="p2601">Pollard, pp. 260–261.</ref><ref>Frith, pp. 255–259.</ref> Correspondence between the Australian Board and the MCC continued for almost a year.<ref>Douglas, pp. 145–47.</ref>
In the final two Tests, England continued employing bodyline tactics but to a lesser extent than the first three.<ref>Frith, pp. 274, 277, 293.</ref> England won the remaining two matches of the series and thus won the series 4–1. Regarding Bradman, he had his leanest run tally in a series with 396 at an average of 56.57, with just one century and three half centuries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HowSTAT! Player Analysis by Series |url=http://howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Players/PlayerSeries.asp?PlayerID=0225 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090916030049/http://howstat.com/cricket/Statistics/Players/PlayerSeries.asp?PlayerID=0225 |archive-date=16 September 2009 |access-date=15 August 2025 |website=www.howstat.com |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Continued use ====
Bodyline continued to be bowled occasionally in the 1933 English season, most notably by [[Nottinghamshire County Cricket Club|Nottinghamshire]], who had [[Arthur Carr (cricketer)|Carr]], [[Bill Voce|Voce]] and [[Harold Larwood|Larwood]] in their team.<ref name="p141">Perry, p. 141.</ref>

When the West Indies toured England in 1933, their captain [[Jackie Grant]] decided to use bodyline against the English for the first time. The match was drawn, but played a significant part in turning English opinion against bodyline. ''The Times'' used the word bodyline, without using inverted commas or using the qualification ''so-called'', for the first time.<ref name="Douglas168">Douglas, p.168.</ref> ''[[Wisden Cricketers' Almanack|Wisden]]'' wrote that "most of those watching it for the first time must have come to the conclusion that, while strictly within the law, it was not nice."<ref name="Douglas168" /><ref>See ''Cricinfo'' for the [http://www.cricinfo.com/link_to_database/ARCHIVE/1930S/1933/WI_IN_ENG/WI_ENG_T2_22-25JUL1933.html scorecard] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050125024331/http://www.cricinfo.com/link_to_database/ARCHIVE/1930S/1933/WI_IN_ENG/WI_ENG_T2_22-25JUL1933.html |date=25 January 2005 }} of the second Test between England and West Indies in 1933.</ref>

In 1934, Bill Woodfull led Australia back to England in a tour that had been under a cloud since the previous Ashes series. Jardine had retired from International cricket in early 1934 after captaining a fraught tour of India and under England's new captain, [[Bob Wyatt]], agreements were put in place so that bodyline would not be used.<ref name="h84">Haigh and Frith, p. 84.</ref><ref name="ha354">Harte, p. 354.</ref><ref name="r164">Robinson, p. 164.</ref> However, there were occasions when the Australians felt that their hosts had crossed the mark with tactics resembling bodyline.<ref name="h84"/> In a match between the Australians and Nottinghamshire, Voce, one of the bodyline bowlers in 1932–33 again used the tactics. Woodfull told the Nottinghamshire administrators that, if Voce's leg-side bowling was repeated, his men would leave the field and return to London. He further said that Australia would not return to the country in the future.<ref name="r164"/><ref name="h85">Haigh and Frith, p. 85.</ref><ref name="p28-30">Perry, pp. 147–148.</ref><ref>Harte, p. 356.</ref>

==== Outlawing ====
Originally, the MCC hoped that captains would ensure that the game was played in the correct spirit, and passed a resolution that bodyline bowling would breach this spirit.<ref name="Williamson">{{cite web |last=Williamson |first=Martin |title=A brief history ... Bodyline |work=Cricinfo |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/bodyline/content/story/148537.html |access-date=6 March 2013 |publisher=ESPNCricinfo |archive-date=4 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191004065604/http://www.espncricinfo.com/bodyline/content/story/148537.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>Frith, p. 374.</ref> When this proved to be insufficient,<ref name="Williamson" /> the MCC passed a law for the 1935 English cricket season, that "direct attack" bowling was unfair and became the responsibility of the umpires to identify and stop.<ref name="F408">Frith, p. 408.</ref> Later, in 1957, the Laws were altered to prevent more than two fielders standing behind square on the leg side; the intention was to prevent negative bowling tactics whereby off spinners and slow inswing bowlers aimed at the leg stump of batsmen with fielders concentrated on the leg side.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chalke |first1=Stephen |title=No Coward Soul. The remarkable story of Bob Appleyard |last2=Hodgson |first2=Derek |publisher=Fairfield Books |year=2003 |isbn=0-9531196-9-6 |location=Bath |page=177}}</ref> However, an indirect effect was to make bodyline fields impossible to implement.<ref name="Williamson"/>

Later law changes, under the heading of "Intimidatory Short Pitched Bowling", also restricted the number of "[[Bouncer (cricket)|bouncers]]" which could be bowled in an [[Over (cricket)|over]].<ref name="begin">{{cite web |title=A Dummy's Guide to Bodyline |url=http://content-aus.cricinfo.com/bodyline/content/story/316343.html |access-date=31 July 2008 |publisher=[[Cricinfo]] |archive-date=19 January 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130119205934/http://content-aus.cricinfo.com/bodyline/content/story/316343.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>Frith, pp. 10–17.</ref>

=== End of timeless Tests ===
{{Main|Timeless Test}}There were 99 timeless Tests between 1877 and 1939.<ref>John Lazenby, ''Edging Towards Darkness: The Story of the Last Timeless Test'', Bloomsbury, London, 2017, p. 180.</ref> Of these, five were held in England, two in South Africa, one in the West Indies, with the remaining ninety-one being held in Australia. All Tests in Australia were timeless prior to [[World War II]]. The Australian climate combined with groundskeepers leaving the pitch uncovered and watering the pitch well meant pitches would dry out and crack as the match progressed, often making batting difficult by days four or five.<ref>Lazenby, p. 229.</ref> Only two timeless Tests in Australia were drawn, both against England in 1882, when the matches had to be left unfinished due to shipping schedules.<ref>Lazenby, pp. 188–89.</ref>

Timeless Tests were sometimes used outside Australia if the series result depended on the outcome of the match. This happened in [[Kingston, Jamaica|Kingston]] in 1930 when the Fourth (and final) Test between West Indies and England lasted for seven playing days and had to be abandoned owing to shipping schedules. The fifth and final Test at The Oval in 1938 was also timeless, as England batted for the first two and a half days and made 903 for 7, before declaring and dismissing Australia twice by the end of the fourth day.<ref>Lazenby, pp. 187–88.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=4th Test, England tour of West Indies at Kingston, Apr 3–12 1930 |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/series/17590/scorecard/62579/west-indies-vs-england-4th-test-england-tour-of-west-indies-1929-30/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180329190012/http://www.espncricinfo.com/series/17590/scorecard/62579/west-indies-vs-england-4th-test-england-tour-of-west-indies-1929-30/ |archive-date=29 March 2018 |access-date=29 March 2018 |website=Cricinfo}}</ref>
[[File:StateLibQld 1 133529 Athlone Castle (ship).jpg|thumb|300x300px|The [[RMMV Athlone Castle|Athlone Castle]], the ship England needed to catch]]
The fifth and final Test at [[Kingsmead Cricket Ground|Durban]] in 1938–39 between [[South Africa national cricket team|South Africa]] and [[England cricket team|England]] was also timeless. The infamous match was spread over twelve days with nine days of actual play – including two rest days and one day with no play. The match started on Friday 3 March 1939. South Africa batted first and were bowled out for 530 on Monday 6 March, with the Sunday having been a rest day. In reply England were bowled out on Wednesday, 8 March for 316. South Africa extended their lead with 481 in their second innings, as they batted for another two days, setting England a target of 696 to win. England were 0/0 at stumps on Thursday 9 March. At stumps on Friday 10 March, England had reached 253 for the loss of just one wicket. There was no play on Saturday, and Sunday was a rest day. They resumed on Monday, reaching 496 for the loss of three wickets. By 14 March 1939, they had reached 654 for the loss of five wickets in the fourth innings (the highest ever [[First-class cricket|first-class]] fourth innings score)<ref name="Beard">{{cite book |last=Frindall |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Frindall |title=Ask Bearders |publisher=[[BBC Books]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-84607-880-4 |pages=216–217}}</ref> but the match had to remain unfinished as England's had to catch a train to Cape Town where their boat home was due to depart. The match had not been expected to take more than five days, but rain and rolling rejuvenated the pitch three times during the match, and it was still in good condition for batting when the match was abandoned.<ref>Lazenby, pp. 99–181.</ref>

The South Africans suggested that England could make alternative travel arrangements, to allow the match to be finished the next day. Hammond had had enough and disagreed. And so the match was called off. He remarked in his final speech: “I don’t think timeless Test matches are in the best interests of the game, and I sincerely hope that the last one has been played.”<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bull |first=Andy |date=22 December 2015 |title=The Test match that went on and on and on. Without a winner but with meaning |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2015/dec/22/the-spin-cricket-the-timeless-test-1939 |access-date=12 September 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Wisden noted: "the limitless match we now believe to be dead."<ref name=":19">{{Cite web |date=26 November 2015 |title=Changes to Test cricket over the years |url=https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/changes-to-test-cricket-over-the-years/72xnur0tp |access-date=20 September 2025 |website=SBS News |language=en}}</ref>

Timeless Tests were never scheduled after World War II, owing to the scheduling difficulties of matches that could continue indefinitely,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Timeless Test matches: Play until there's a result |url=https://www.theroar.com.au/2020/06/30/timeless-test-matches-play-until-theres-a-result/ |access-date=12 September 2025 |website=The Roar |language=en-US |archive-date=24 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224103504/https://www.theroar.com.au/2020/06/30/timeless-test-matches-play-until-theres-a-result/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and the comparative dullness of the play.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bull |first=Andy |date=19 July 2011 |title=The return of the timeless Tests |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2011/jul/19/the-spin-return-timeless-tests |access-date=12 September 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Admission of Pakistan ===
[[File:Abdul Hafeez Kardar and Lala Amarnath with President of India Rajendra Prasad.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Captains [[Abdul Hafeez Kardar|Abdul Kardar]] (left) and [[Lala Amarnath]] (right) with Indian President [[Rajendra Prasad]] (centre) on the day of the first test, 16 October 1952]]On 28 July 1952, Pakistan were admitted to the ICC, and in October that year played their first Test match.<ref>{{Cite web |last=icc |title=1909–1963 – Imperial Cricket Conference {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1909-1963 |access-date=12 September 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=22 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240222135726/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1909-1963 |url-status=live }}</ref> Almost 30 years passed until the next member (Sri Lanka) joined.

=== Five Day Tests in England ===
In 1948, matches in England were scheduled over five days for the first time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goodman |first=Tom |date=14 August 2019 |title=From the Archives: Bradman out for 'duck' in his last Test |url=https://www.smh.com.au/sport/cricket/from-the-archives-bradman-out-for-duck-in-his-last-test-20190716-p527r0.html |access-date=12 September 2025 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en |archive-date=20 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220120181629/https://www.smh.com.au/sport/cricket/from-the-archives-bradman-out-for-duck-in-his-last-test-20190716-p527r0.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Chronology of cricket – Bloomsbury |url=https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/discover/wisden/archive/chronology-of-cricket/ |access-date=12 September 2025 |website=www.bloomsbury.com |archive-date=5 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221005223022/https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/discover/wisden/archive/chronology-of-cricket/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Most matches from 1880 to 1949 were three days, and from 1950 all matches were scheduled for five days except for the 2019 Test between England and Ireland (which was four days) and final matches of series in 1953, 1972 and 1975, which were six days. The [[World Test Championship]] final in 2021 was scheduled for five days with a reserve day, which was used after the first day was lost to rain.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Days allocated to Men's Test Cricket in England – The ACS |url=https://acscricket.com/?page_id=6708 |access-date=12 September 2025 |language=en-GB |archive-date=20 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250320174325/https://acscricket.com/?page_id=6708 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 8 March 1955, the ICC made the following decision at their meeting:<ref name=":8" />

{{Blockquote|text=In future all members of the Imperial Cricket Conference visiting England will play five five-day Test Matches. This will bring India, West Indies, New Zealand and Pakistan into line for the first time with Australia and South Africa.|author=}}

=== Advent of covered pitches ===
Various levels of "covering" existed through the history of cricket, from the Laws in 1884—"The ground shall not be rolled, watered, covered, mown, or beaten during a match, except before the commencement of each innings and of each day’s play." This phrasing remained until the 1947 Laws, which stated the pitch should not be covered "unless special regulations so provide". These Laws also permitted covering the run-ups to the pitch. The next edition of the Laws, in 1980, allowed for "complete covering of the pitch" before a match, but not during "unless prior arrangement or regulations so provide."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Ebor |first=Old |date=17 May 2022 |title=The Extinction of the Sticky Wicket: The Confusing History of Pitch Covering |url=https://oldebor.wordpress.com/2022/05/17/the-extinction-of-the-sticky-wicket-the-confusing-history-of-pitch-covering/ |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=Old Ebor |language=en}}</ref>

The main issue with uncovered pitches was that it produced "sticky wickets", which occurred after rain, while the pitch was drying, especially when this happened quickly. On a genuine sticky wicket, players could expect the ball to turn sharply with just a small amount of spin on the ball. Some balls might deviate a significant amount, while others would skid through. There was also often extremely uneven bounce.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last=Ebor |first=Old |date=10 May 2022 |title=The Sticky Wicket: How rain used to influence cricket pitches |url=https://oldebor.wordpress.com/2022/05/10/the-sticky-wicket-how-rain-used-to-influence-cricket-pitches/ |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=Old Ebor |language=en |archive-date=1 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250901212409/https://oldebor.wordpress.com/2022/05/10/the-sticky-wicket-how-rain-used-to-influence-cricket-pitches/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Leaving pitches uncovered also meant rain would cause huge delays while the ground dried out enough to permit play. The loss of time and gate money was of huge concern to administrators, especially those with precarious finances.<ref name=":10" />

Due to several wet summers, after much discussion, from the beginning of the [[1959 English cricket season|1959 season]], full covering was made compulsory for County cricket and Test matches.<ref name=":9" /> The entire pitch had to be covered every evening and on Sundays, it also had to be covered whenever play was abandoned due to rain. The only instance where pitches were not covered was when players came off due to rain but play was not abandoned.

From the 1960s and 70s, uncovered pitches across the world began to be phased out.<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 April 2018 |title=Pushing the (sealed) envelope: An alternative to the coin toss |url=https://www.wisden.com/cricket-news/a-good-toss-to-lose-david-franklin-pushes-crickets-sealed-envelope |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=Wisden |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Covered pitches |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-covered-pitches-461172 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603232219/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-covered-pitches-461172 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1960, the first full covering during a Test was used in England.<ref name=":9" /> However, regulations were sometimes vague and even contradictory.<ref name=":9" /> The final changes came in the 1970s. In 1979, Test matches in England had total pitch covering during rain.<ref name=":9" /> The end of sticky wickets came in 1981 when the same full covering was enforced in all English first-class matches.<ref name=":9" />

After these changes, pitches became more standardised across the world, although differences still remained between countries and even between venues, due to the type of soil used and the local climate.<ref>{{Cite news |last=McGarry |first=Andrew |date=26 November 2015 |title=Innovations that changed the game of cricket |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2015-11-26/innovations-that-changed-cricket/6977816 |access-date=13 September 2025 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU |archive-date=27 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240227112536/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2015-11-26/innovations-that-changed-cricket/6977816 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=14 January 2022 |title=The science of cricket pitch soil |url=https://cosmosmagazine.com/people/culture/cricket-pitch-soil-science-wicket/ |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=cosmosmagazine.com |language=en-AU |archive-date=13 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250613224211/https://cosmosmagazine.com/people/culture/cricket-pitch-soil-science-wicket/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Climate phenomenon catches England cricketers out down under – University of Reading |url=https://archive.reading.ac.uk/news-events/2009/June/pr21992.html |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=archive.reading.ac.uk}}</ref>

=== Imperial Cricket Conference renamed International Cricket Conference ===
On 15 July 1965, the Imperial Cricket Conference renamed itself the International Cricket Conference and countries from all over the world could be admitted, instead of only commonwealth countries.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=The ICC becomes democratic |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-the-icc-becomes-democratic-514060 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240422033549/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-the-icc-becomes-democratic-514060 |archive-date=22 April 2024 |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=icc |title=1964–1988 – International Cricket Conference {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1964-1988 |access-date=13 September 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=14 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214102554/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1964-1988 |url-status=live }}</ref> Despite this, it was still run as an exclusive club by English cricket–the MCC president was the ICC president and the MCC secretary was the ICC secretary.<ref name=":11" />

=== Suspension of South Africa (1970–1991) ===
{{See also|Sporting boycott of South Africa during the apartheid era}}

==== Apartheid ====
{{Main|Apartheid}}
Globally, tensions were rising throughout the 1960s against the [[apartheid]] regime of the South African government. Sporting boycotts due to the regime were enacted in the 1960s as countries across the world showed their condemnation of racial segregation.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |title=When politics killed a tour |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-to-1970-when-politics-killed-a-tour-571799 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250119201635/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/rewind-to-1970-when-politics-killed-a-tour-571799 |archive-date=19 January 2025 |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> South Africa left the [[Commonwealth of Nations]] in 1961, and per the rules of the time, therefore had to leave the ICC.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=History of Cricket |url=https://archive.thedailystar.net/campus/2007/02/04/feature_cricket.htm |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=archive.thedailystar.net |archive-date=2 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231202111919/https://archive.thedailystar.net/campus/2007/02/04/feature_cricket.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== D'Oliveira affair ====
[[File:Anti-apartheidsdemonstratie in Amsterdam de kop van de demonstratie, Bestanddeelnr 934-2645.jpg|thumb|300x300px|Anti-apartheid protest in [[Amsterdam]], 1988]]
{{Main|D'Oliveira affair}}
In 1968, Basil d'Oliveira, a mixed-race South African player who had represented England since 1966, was prohibited from playing by the South African government, in a development known as the [[D'Oliveira affair]]. The British prime minister at the time, [[Harold Wilson]] remarked: "Once the South Africans had said that they were not taking a player [d'Oliveira] we wanted to send, I would have rather thought that put them beyond the pale of civilized cricket."<ref name="booth98p99">Booth 1998 [[iarchive:racegamesportpol0000boot/page/99|p. 99]]</ref> Due to the affair, the English tour of South Africa was cancelled.<ref name=":12" />

==== Cancelled 1970 tour ====
{{Main|South African cricket team in England in 1970 (proposed)}}
Eighteen months later, South Africa was due to tour England as part of the 1970 season, and the public was growing discontent with the prospect of the tour,<ref name=":12" /> meanwhile the game's administrators remained steadfast in its determination that the tour should go ahead.<ref name=":12" /> Minutes of several meetings of the ICC and MCC showed they were much more concerned with the upcoming metrication in the UK and subsequent changing of the pitch length from 22 yards to 20.12 metres, and the weight of the ball from 5.5 ounces to 155.8 grams.<ref name=":12" /> On 12 December 1969, the Test and County Cricket Board (the precursor to the [[England and Wales Cricket Board|ECB]]) confirmed the tour would proceed, adding it was "averse to racial discrimination of any kind ... and respected the right of those who wish to demonstrate peacefully." However, at that stage protests had escalated from being peaceful.<ref name=":12" /> By the end of January 1970, twelve county grounds had been vandalised.

On 30 January, the [[International Cavaliers]], a touring charity-based multi-racial cricket team, had been refused entry to South Africa. A letter from the South African Cricket Association ended with "you must be aware any tour ... including non-white personnel would not be allowed." The MCC tried to distance itself from the situation, claiming that the Cavaliers were a private organisation; this only served to make itself appear woefully out of touch with the world.<ref name=":12" />

By mid-February, the MCC had cut the schedule from 28 to 11 matches, as they removed grounds seen as impossible to protect. They even permitted laying of artificial pitches on grounds hosting games, in order to allow play to continue if they were vandalised during play.<ref name=":12" /> Both pro and anti-tour letters were sent to newspapers as the tour grew closer, with players and officials taking stances for or against. Some journalists refused to commentate on any of the games; one, [[John Arlott]], said that while he was not sure protests at games were the answer, he felt that by allowing the tour to go ahead the ICC had put cricket in a position where it would be "the ultimate and inevitable sufferer" and that the Tests "would offer comfort and confirmation to a completely evil regime."

==== Ban ====
In April, Harold Wilson told the BBC that the MCC had made "a big mistake" in allowing the tour to happen. "Everyone should be free to demonstrate against apartheid ... I hope people will feel free to do so." In early May, the annual meeting of the MCC backed the tour without requiring a vote. Later, Warwickshire said they wouldn't pick any of their three coloured players for the match against the South Africans. The following day the gates at [[Edgbaston Cricket Ground|Edgbaston]] were vandalised.<ref name=":12" /> On 20 May 12 days before the first match, the ICC voted almost unanimously for the tour to go ahead. "It was agreed in the long term this policy was in the best interests of cricket, and of cricketers of all races in South Africa," proclaimed secretary [[Billy Griffith]]. Despite this, the ICC stated there would be no further series involving South Africa "until SA cricket is played and teams selected on a multi-racial basis." An editorial in the Daily Mirror wrote: "The rulers of cricket stonewall on ... if this is their last word, they are assuming a terrible responsibility." On 22 May,<ref>{{Cite news |date=22 May 1970 |title=1970: South Africa cricket tour called off |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/may/22/newsid_2504000/2504573.stm |access-date=19 September 2025 |language=en-GB |archive-date=7 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080307133241/http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/may/22/newsid_2504000/2504573.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> the ICC called the tour off "with great regret", following a strongly worded official request from James Callaghan, the British home secretary. Griffith said he "regretted the discourtesy" to the South African board and further said he "deplored the activities of those who intimidate."

Inside the British government, there were fears the tour would cause racial unrest within the country, and allowing the tour to carry on could only harm Wilson's chances of re-election. John Vorster, South Africa's prime minister was furious. "For a government to submit so easily and so willingly to open blackmail is to me unbelievable." [[Ali Bacher]], South Africa's captain was more reserved: "I regret the manner in which politics have become involved in cricket ... [but] unless we broaden our outlook we will remain forever in isolation." That isolation lasted longer than anyone feared as the ICC's members voted to suspend South Africa indefinitely from international cricket at their meeting.<ref name=":13" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=icc |title=History of Cricket in the 20th Century {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/cricket/history-of-cricket/20th-century |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=20 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520193911/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/cricket/history-of-cricket/20th-century |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Rebel tours ====
{{Main|South African rebel tours}}
Following the ban from the ICC, [[South African rebel tours|rebel tours]] took place in the 1980s, in spite of the express disapproval of the national cricket boards and governments, the ICC, and international organisations such as the [[United Nations]]<ref>Pg 35–71, Peter May, ''The Rebel Tours: Cricket's Crisis of Conscience'', 2009</ref> They were the subject of enormous controversy and remain a sensitive topic in the cricket world. Many players from various countries were banned for some years for their involvement in the rebel tours.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Humphries |first=Gary Linnell and David |date=26 July 2019 |title=From the Archives. 1985: Rebel cricketers banned for tours of South Africa |url=https://www.smh.com.au/sport/cricket/from-the-archives-1985-rebel-cricketers-banned-for-tours-of-south-africa-20190726-p52b6l.html |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en |archive-date=18 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240718030613/https://www.smh.com.au/sport/cricket/from-the-archives-1985-rebel-cricketers-banned-for-tours-of-south-africa-20190726-p52b6l.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Mason |first=Peter |date=6 November 2024 |title=The 1983 West Indian rebel tour to South Africa that shocked cricket |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2024/nov/06/cricket-west-indies-rebel-tour-1983-south-africa-clyde-walcott |access-date=19 September 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Williamson |first=Martin |date=13 November 2009 |title=The Dirty Dozen |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/the-dirty-dozen-434386 |website=ESPNCricinfo |access-date=20 September 2025 |archive-date=29 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250629105431/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/the-dirty-dozen-434386 |url-status=live }}</ref> The English cricket side that toured South Africa in 1981–82 became known as "The Dirty Dozen".

==== Re-admission ====
In 1991, the ICC re-admitted South Africa at the personal request of [[Nelson Mandela]], ending the 22 year ban.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Odendaal |first=Andre |date=20 June 2010 |title=South Africa are isolated |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-south-africa-are-isolated-463657 |website=ESPNCricinfo |access-date=20 September 2025 |archive-date=1 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250401030558/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/cricket-s-turning-points-south-africa-are-isolated-463657 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== 6-ball over standardised globally ===
During the first 100 years of Test cricket, the number of balls per [[Over (cricket)|over]] ranged between 4 and 8.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |title=History of Overs – Test Cricket |url=https://www.howstat.com/Cricket/Statistics/Misc/HistoryOvers.asp |website=Howstat |access-date=20 September 2025 |archive-date=27 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240927050157/https://howstat.com/Cricket/Statistics/Misc/HistoryOvers.asp |url-status=live }}</ref> While matches in England had used 6-ball overs since 1946, and in South Africa since 1961–62, Pakistan, New Zealand and Australia had used 8-ball overs for several years. In 1978–79, Pakistan switched to 6-ball overs, and Australia and New Zealand switched the following season from 1979–80, standardising over length globally.<ref name=":15" />

There is no recorded reason for the switching between four, five, six, and eight ball overs in the formative years of cricket, however it is understood that the shortness of four and five-ball overs meant there were too many over changes during the course of the day, and also made it difficult for bowlers to get into a rhythm to plot a dismissal.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |date=6 June 2008 |title=That's the over |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/that-s-the-over-353235 |access-date=20 September 2025 |website=ESPNCricinfo |archive-date=7 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207031925/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/that-s-the-over-353235 |url-status=live }}</ref> Eight-ball overs were used in Australia in an attempt to get more balls bowled in a day's play due to the reduction in change-overs. However, a downside was that bowlers would slow down in self preservation.<ref name=":14" /> The ICC permitted both 6-ball and 8-ball overs in the Laws, depending on the conditions of play in the host country. From the 2000 Laws, only 6-ball overs were permitted.<ref name=":13" />

It is widely believed that with the commercialisation of cricket and the [[Packer Revolution|Packer revolution]], there was no room left for the 8-ball over and the 6-ball over provided a happy balance between over changes and rhythm for the bowlers.<ref name=":14" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Fella |first=Full On |date=18 February 2025 |title=Cricket Hasn't Always had Six Balls Per Over – Full on Sport |url=https://www.fullonsport.co.uk/cricket-hasnt-always-had-six-balls-per-over/ |access-date=19 September 2025 |language=en-US |archive-date=19 June 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250619034732/https://www.fullonsport.co.uk/cricket-hasnt-always-had-six-balls-per-over/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Admission of Sri Lanka and Zimbabwe, and further changes to the ICC ===
On 21 July 1981, Sri Lanka was admitted by the ICC as a full member, becoming the eighth Test playing nation. They played their first Test match [[English cricket team in Sri Lanka in 1981–82#Only Test|against England]] at [[Paikiasothy Saravanamuttu Stadium|P. Sara Oval]], Colombo on 17 February 1982.<ref>{{cite web |title=First Test match for Sri Lanka |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci/engine/match/63307.html |access-date=5 August 2016 |work=ESPN Cricinfo |archive-date=26 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226135239/http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci/engine/match/63307.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In July 1989, the International Cricket Conference renamed itself to the International Cricket Council. In the same year, the practice of the MCC President automatically assuming the chairmanship of the ICC came to an end, though with the election of [[Colin Cowdrey]], was still led by an Englishman.<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=icc |title=1989–Present – International Cricket Council {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1989-present |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=16 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210816142659/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1989-present |url-status=live }}</ref> The renamed organisation had more teeth; it was no longer confined to just making recommendations to national governing bodies, but could impose binding decisions on members.<ref name=":16" />

In July 1992, Zimbabwe was admitted by the ICC as a full member, becoming the ninth Test playing nation. They played their first Test match in October that year, against [[India national cricket team|India]] at [[Harare Sports Club]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Only Test: Zimbabwe v India at Harare, Oct 18–22, 1992 |url=http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci/engine/current/match/63583.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111023202744/http://www.espncricinfo.com/ci/engine/current/match/63583.html |archive-date=23 October 2011 |access-date=5 November 2011 |work=Cricinfo |publisher=[[ESPNcricinfo]]}}</ref>

1993 saw the creation of the Chief Executive of ICC, to which David Richards of the Australian Cricket Board was appointed. With his appointment, the practice of the MCC's secretary performing the same function for the ICC came to an end.<ref name=":16" />

=== Television replays, return of South Africa, neutral umpires and admission of Bangladesh ===
{{Main|Third umpire}}
The [[Indian cricket team in South Africa in 1992–93|Indian tour of South Africa in 1992–93]] marked the first use of television replays in Test cricket, and was also the first Test series played by South Africa after their ban by the ICC 23 years previous.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web |title=A historic tour in more ways than one |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/a-historic-tour-in-more-ways-than-one-87448 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241215025411/https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/a-historic-tour-in-more-ways-than-one-87448 |archive-date=15 December 2024 |access-date=20 September 2025 |website=ESPNcricinfo |language=en |url-status=live }}</ref> The tour was also known for the trialling of [[Elite Panel of ICC Umpires|independent umpires]].<ref name=":17" /><ref name=":19" /> Television replays were used to settle "awkward line decisions" which morphed into the [[third umpire]] provision.<ref name=":17" /><ref name=":18">{{Cite news |title=SOUTH AFRICA v INDIA 1992–93 |url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/wisdenalmanack/content/story/153619.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208055338/https://www.espncricinfo.com/wisdenalmanack/content/story/153619.html |archive-date=8 December 2024 |access-date=20 September 2025 |work=Cricinfo |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Sachin Tendulkar]] was the first player to be given out, run out, by the third umpire.

By 1995, it had been agreed that television replays should be available in Tests "wherever possible" and that the third umpire should signal out with a red light, and not out with a green light (Tendulkar was given out with a green light in the first Test at Durban in November 1992.<ref name=":18" />)

In 1996, cameras were also permitted to check whether a ball had crossed the boundary, and in 1997, umpires could call on the third umpire to check if a catch was clean or not.<ref>{{Cite web |last=icc |title=1989–Present – International Cricket Council {{!}} About ICC Cricket |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1989-present |access-date=20 September 2025 |website=icc |language=en |archive-date=16 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210816142659/https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/the-icc/history-of-icc/1989-present |url-status=live }}</ref>

Test Match Playing Conditions in 1998–99 contained the following rules:<ref>{{Cite web |title=Test Match Playing Conditions |url=https://i.imgci.com/link_to_database/ABOUT_CRICKET/ICC_1998-99/TEST_MATCH_PLAYING_CONDITIONS.html |access-date=20 September 2025 |website=i.imgci.com}}</ref>
